utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, everybody. [French interpretation coming over English channel].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, however, that on the transcript, it's good morning, everybody, French interpretation coming over English channel. I hope that is not a problem. I don't think it is. If it is a problem, could the interpreters please confirm? It's fine. Okay, fine. Thank you. All the accused are here. General Pandurevic is back. Defence teams, I only notice the absence of Mr. Meek and Ms. Nikolic. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey. The witness is here, but before I come to you, General, and say good morning, there are two small issues that I would like to address. There is a motion from the Prosecution for the testimony of witness number 88 to be heard via videolink. This was filed on the 25th of May. I don't know exactly when the fortnight lapses. Could I kindly ask you to file your response as early as possible? I know that some of you will not be here in the course of next week. I had in mind -- I had in mind the -- not later than the 12th of June so that we give at least three weeks for the Prosecution to be able to organise this, if the motion is granted. All right? 12th June is all right for everyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can assure the Trial Chamber that we will file it before the 12th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The other thing is that yesterday the Prosecution filed a motion to amend the 65 ter exhibit list with nine exhibits pertaining to witness number 4. Now, this witness is scheduled, according to me, at least, to come after -- not after this witness but after the next one. Is he still scheduled to come over after the next one or not? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That witness was our investigator, Mr. Blaszczyk and he was our sort of insurance witness for this week, which we're probably not going to get to so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So we can allow the Defence teams to file their response at their pleasure and leisure but within the fortnight, okay? All right. So there is no urgency there. Good morning to you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make an effort to conclude your testimony today. It also depends on you, particularly on how concise you can keep your answers. Madam Fauveau, you had the floor yesterday. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness Exhibit number 5D372?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you said that fuel was sometimes smuggled in the double-sided tanks in humanitarian convoys and UNPROFOR convoys. Please look at the document and tell us if you can confirm whether this document was sent to the Sarajevo Corps and the Drina Corps on the 8th of November 1994.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I shall leave you some time to peruse this document because I would like you to confirm for us that this document states that there are double-sided tanks in the vehicles. Can you see the part where it says that it is well known that there were cases of abuse when it came to the bottom part of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have already said yes for this document. This is one in a series of documents of which I spoke yesterday. Whenever we discovered something suspicious or whenever it was proven at check-points that our suspicion was justified, we had to draw the attention of UNPROFOR and UNHCR to those facts and as for the Drina and Herzegovina corps and here the Sarajevo Corps as well because from the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Corps the convoys usually departed from the sector of Sarajevo. I was reading the document and I have forgotten what you want me to tell you. What do you want me to confirm?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that this document requires more stringent control of the vehicles and especially its bottom part?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now I would like to show the witness Exhibit number 5D380. Is it true that this document is information that was sent to the corps of the VRS on the 18th of December 1993, and it regards the permission to allow for the passage of convoys?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was sent to all corps save for the 2nd Krajina Corps because the -- no convoys passed through their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now go to page 7 of this document, please? I believe that there is a relevant part at the very beginning of the page. Sir, do you see the part which is under number 1, immediately below the title, the title is, "Attention to all corps." Is it true that this passage calls for a very precise control of all humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is one in a series of such warnings whenever something suspicious was discovered.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And can we now scroll down to the bottom of the document? I would like the witness to be able to see item number 4. Item 4, a bit further up. Yes. Is it true that special attention should have been drawn to the convoys headed for Gorazde, Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because those were enclaves unlike other security areas, which were connected with other territories. For example, Tuzla was connected with the territory under the control of Muslims. The same applied to Sarajevo and Bihac said -- Bihac had a territorial connection with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now show the witness 6D7? And before this document appears on the screen, I would like to tell you that this is a decision by the president of the republic, published in the Official Gazette on the 14th of March 1995. Can we show page 2 to the witness, the second page, please. What I'm interested in is the title under number 28. This is a decision on the establishment of the state committee on cooperation with the United Nations and humanitarian organisations. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now show the witness Article 5 on the same page? Can we go back to -- According to this article, one of the working bodies of this committee was the coordination body for humanitarian operations, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke about that yesterday, but I was not sure of the month and now I can see that this was the month of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now show the witness Article number 6 in the same document? Sir, is it true that the article reads as follows: "[In English] Permit for the movement of convoys and employees of the UN and humanitarian organisations on the territory of Republika Srpska shall be issued by the coordinating body for humanitarian operations pursuant to committee decisions"?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, which means that the army of Republika Srpska lost that obligation. Up to then, we were the ones to issue such permits and the obligation was passed on to the committee and we were just the executers of the committee's decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the first page of this document? Can we blow up the top part of this page featuring the date? The very top of the page, please. This is the Official Gazette published on the 14th of March 1995. In other words, it was published after directive number 7 was issued.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directive number 7, as far as I can remember, was issued on the 8th of March, and this decision was passed on the 11th of March, as far as I could see at the bottom, and it was published on the Official Gazette on the 14th of March, which means that it was indeed published after the publication of directive number 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, after the publication of this decision, the army of Republika Srpska merely carried out orders by this committee and performed procedures and controls in agreement with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the army of Republika Srpska no longer had to agree upon anything with UNPROFOR. This was the duty of the committee. And the committee simply issued orders to the army to let convoys through and to perform controls. In other words, we could no longer decide, we could no longer make a decision on whether we were going to let a convoy through or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In any case, the army continued to control the convoys?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit number P2427 -- 2497. The document that is now in front of you is information sent to the military post 7111 with regard to the passage of the convoy on the 18th of June 1995. That is the date indicated on the document.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What am I supposed to confirm or deny with regard to this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is this indeed information which was sent to the military post 7111, in which this post is informed about the passage of a convoy and was this information sent on the 18th of June 1995?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is correct. I can't remember the military post 7111. I suppose that this was the command of either eastern Bosnia or the Drina Corps, since the convoy was on its way from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I believe that this was the Drina Corps because the convoy was supposed to enter through Karakaj and Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this information was certainly drafted pursuant to a decision of the committee which was in charge of humanitarian operations?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could see the entire document to get an idea of the drafter at the end of it? The screen doesn't show it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. Is it possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm going to move to page 2 because I have questions about that page, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's move straight to page 2, please, which we have on the monitor now. Go ahead. He had started to answer your question. I take it that he only answered it in part. General, Madam Fauveau asked you, and this information was certainly drafted pursuant to a decision of the committee that was in charge of humanitarian operations? And you started by saying, "Correct" and then you said "only." You were seeking trying to explain something else. Could you proceed and give us your explanation, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The author of the document did not link the document with any source. Usually, military documents are drafted in the following way: Pursuant to a decision of this and that body, this information was obviously drafted based on somebody's decision. So the author should have stated this: "Pursuant to the decision of the committee" or "pursuant to the decision of anybody who provided this information to the Main Staff." So this is a shortcoming that arose from the lack of skills. I can see that General Miletic in his own hand stated on behalf of the Chief of Staff, Colonel Radivoje Miletic. On that date, I was in the western parts of Bosnia, probably in Drvar. In other words, the only shortcoming of this document is that it doesn't show the source based on which the document was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Speaking of the penultimate paragraph of this document, which is right in front of you, calling for better control, is it the case that this control was in fact in keeping with the previously adopted rules and regulations concerning the passage of convoys?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This paragraph follows from previous documents we have reviewed, but regardless of the fact that actual people on the ground who were effecting those controls have been warned already, in our language we say it's never too much care or better safe than sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that such controls are neither unusual nor odd in a state of war?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nothing irregular or unusual. This was agreed back in 1992 when it was decided to bring humanitarian aid to the warring parties in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But General Miletic, then Colonel, in any case, did not have the power to decide whether a convoy would be allowed to pass or not?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document, nobody from the army had any more power to decide whether the convoy would pass or not. It was up to the committee. And Miletic and other officers in the army were duty-bound to see that convoy and inspect it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show the witness 5D371 -- sorry, just before that, are you sure that the handwriting on this document is the handwriting of General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. General Miletic knows better.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now show 5D371 to the witness? Could you please look at first paragraph only? We don't see the date on this document, but I believe that in the first paragraph we can read that it is about a medical evacuation that was authorised from Srebrenica to Sarajevo on the 6th of April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see 6 April 1995. I see my signature, in fact, my full name, typed there, which I think is possible because in April I was at the Main Staff. I see again this military PO box, 7111 and 7598, but I don't remember those PO boxes. I don't know what exactly one would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please read this first paragraph that follows after the numbers of PO boxes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we do that, I notice that there is a discrepancy between the original and the English translation. The English translation merely indicates to military post 7111 so -- oh, this is a different one, yeah, okay. All right. Then my next question is: We see 7111 and then an "i," and then 7598. What's that "i"? What does it stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the "i" that we discussed yesterday. It's going to those two military post boxes only: 7111 and 7598. Those must be the Sarajevo and the Drina Corps, because the evacuation of this woman Fatima Salihovic was to take the route Vlasenica-Zvornik-Bratunac, if I'm reading correctly. Or maybe I'm confused. I believe this lady was evacuated from Srebrenica to Sarajevo. Yes, that's written there. So the command of the corps, through whose territory this vehicle would pass, are being informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you see those two numbers with an "i" in between, to you it means letter box 7111 and letter box 7598? That is both of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And also other corps are left out of this notification. This was addressed only to those two units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I apologise to you, Madam Fauveau, for having interrupted your question, which you can now proceed with, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, in this paragraph that you just read, that speaks of this medical evacuation, do you see in line 3 the date, 6 April 1995 [realtime transcript read in error "2005"]?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a reference to the commands to whom the documents are addressed indicating the time when the evacuation would take place, and we see below that it was actually sent on the 5th of April, 24 hours earlier, at 2000 something hours. It doesn't matter, anyway. So this document follows an earlier agreement between the UNPROFOR and the VRS that notifications be submitted 24 hours earlier, with 24 hours' notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just one correction. Page 11, line 3 and the date is 6 April 1995. So this evacuation that was authorised on the 5th of April 1995 was authorised after the delivery of directive number 7?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Almost a month later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to move on to another subject, namely the combat reports that you discussed yesterday and the day before yesterday. I would like to show you P2672. I would like to show the witness the top of this document. You have already spoken about this document and you said it was sent to the Drina Corps. Is it correct that this document was not sent to the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said yesterday was that I don't know whether it was sent on to the Main Staff by the command of the Drina Corps, but I checked. It was not sent from the Main Staff to the Supreme Command. So the command of the Drina Corps was the link. I don't know whether the command of the Drina Corps sent this report to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you speak of the reports sent by the Drina Corps, in fact the Drina Corps would not physically send on this report. It would just take up this information from this report?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that this document, in this form, the way we see it, was sent by the Drina Corps to the Main Staff. I said I didn't know whether the Drina Corps informed the Main Staff of the things it had learned from this Engineering Battalion because I don't have any reports from the Drina Corps to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This one is regular, daily report, from the battalion. Is it correct that this information should have been reflected, taken up, in the daily reports of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, because it's a large number of people killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this report is of 4th July 1995 -- 14th July?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what's written there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we show the witness now 4D84, which is also P137? What you have before you now, is it the report of the Drina Corps dated 14 July 1995, addressed to the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the report of which I said I didn't know its contents, but now I see it, and I see that there is a reference to a group -- sorry, this is not about Gorazde. Just give me a minute. Yes. In paragraph 1, we read, "On the northwestern part of the front, in the broader area of Kalesija," in brackets we see the details, Pohunjak, Osredak, Kurtici, "Observers have noted large concentration of enemy forces aiming to attack from the front and thus enable link-up with the group that had broken out from Srebrenica enclave." Now, I suppose that that is the group. I'm not sure. But we don't see here the number mentioned by the commander of the engineering battalion, namely 1.000 to 1.500 people killed, which means that the Main Staff was not aware of that information provided by the engineering battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now show the witness P49? It's a report of the Main Staff of the 15th of July 1995 that you had occasion to see the day before yesterday, and I would like page 3, please, the passage just under number 6. So it's a report in which there is reference to Turkish forces. You've already said that you didn't know how this reference to Turkish forces found its way into the document, how this expression was used. Is it probable that the person who drafted this report at the Main Staff simply took up the phrase from the report sent them by the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if you could show me the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we then move to page 4, the next one?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who the person drafting this, according to these initials, could be. I suppose it's Colonel Nedeljko Trkulja, initials NT. I suppose he just copied this phrase, Turkish forces, I don't know from where, but I already told you yesterday that we freely traded insults. We called Muslims Turks. They called us Chetniks. Both of us called Croats Ustashas, and Croats called us Chetniks and they called Muslims either Turks or something even worse that I don't want to mention. .

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you the interim report of 15 July 1995 from the Drina Corps, and I would like it placed on the ELMO so that the witness can compare the two documents. It's P150. And if we could go back to page 3 in P49? Could you please look at the document on your right and find the sentence that reads, "[In English] During the transport towards Zvornik the Turkish pulling out from Srebrenica toward Tuzla in the Planinci village sector opened fire on the ambulance and killed the driver Milos Tesic and paramedic Nenad Stevic. The brigade will forward details on enemy groups in a separate report about which we will be duly informed." [Interpretation] This sentence is in the document. Did you find it? Did you find the sentence?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? On the left screen or on the right screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We are talking about P150, so I don't know where it is.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an interim report?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is an interim report issued by the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the sentence, "The attack ended around 5.30 but the enemy continued to open fire sporadically from artillery and infantry weapons. During these operations three soldiers were wounded, Velimor Peric, Dusan Stevanovic and Zoran Ristic. During the transport towards Zvornik the Turk forces which were pulling out from Zvornik towards Tuzla in the Planinci mountain sector opened fire on the ambulance and killed the driver, Milos Tesic and the paramedic, Nenad Stevic. The information on the enemy groups that are pulling out from Srebrenica will be provided in a special report." Is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is the sentence. Does it fully reflect the report of the Main Staff? Was it taken over completely from that report, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is an interim report by the corps command to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I believe that we've had a problem in the interpretation. Is it correct that the report of the Main Staff took over virtually completely a sentence that can be found in the interim report of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should be able to see the stamps, the four angled stamps on both reports to see when the reports arrived, and then I will -- would be able to answer your question. This is interim report and interim reports were allowed, pursuant to the organisation of the army. There was a document which stated that regular reports should be sent every day by 2000 hours and interim reports as needed. Obviously this interim report was drafted because of the people who were wounded and killed. This was the reason for the interim report.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I don't think that the report of the Main Staff carries that kind of stamp but the interim report of the Drina Corps does have a stamp towards the very end of the page.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, could I have a look at the regular report of the Main Staff? Could I see the signature part?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please first look -- I'm sorry. Both have stamps, but can you please look at the stamp on the report by the Drina Corps first?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This report was signed by General Major Radislav Krstic. It was received on the 15th of July at 1945 hours, and now I should see when the Main Staff report was sent to the Supreme Command, and I'm talking about the report on the right-hand side screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we scroll up the page or scroll down to enable the witness to see the stamp?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the stamp. The report of the Main Staff to the Supreme Command was sent on the 16th of July on the following day, that is at 0207 hours. The difference in time is approximately five hours, if my maths are good. Somewhere in this report of the Main Staff to the Supreme Command, I saw losses. It is possible that the interim report of the Drina Corps was included in that report but the author of the report to the Supreme Command did not mention the names of the casualties. He just mentioned the numbers of the wounded and the killed. It was not customary to report to the Supreme Command the individual names of the casualties. You can only imagine how far that would leave. For example, if the troops suffered casualties of 50 or 60 killed and as many wounded, it would really be too much to mention all of their names in the reports to the Supreme Command. And let me conclude: I believe that this interim report of the Drina Corps was included in the regular combat report of the Main Staff to the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The day before yesterday, you spoke about the nature of combat reports. Can we please show the witness the first page of the document? Is it correct that this combat report was not sent only to the Supreme Command but also to the commands of all corps of the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that in the heading, the commands of the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, the Sarajevo Corps, the Drina Corps, the aircraft, anti-aircraft defence, in other words, to all subordinate units. I suppose that General Miletic intended to inform about such specific situations, even the subordinate units because the Main Staff doesn't send any reports to subordinated commands. It rather receives reports from them and when it writes to them it sends them decisions and orders. I suppose the duplication of resources was avoided by copying this report to the subordinated units which was a customary thing. When something extraordinary was happening, all the units were informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now show the witness the last page of the same document? This document has not been signed, but the name on this report is the name of General Miletic, and his role was described as standing in for the Chief of Staff. The day before yesterday, you told us that your name was supposed to be on these reports because at that time you were the Chief of Staff of the VRS, and the person who signed these reports should have put the word "za" or on behalf of in front of their signature?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, Miletic wanted to make sure that everybody knew that this was his document so he came up with something. He could not put VD, acting for. This is a legal category which had to be covered by an order. He could have put replacing the Chief of Staff or something. He came up with standing in for the Chief of Staff. We've discussed this at great length. The important thing is that the signatory of this document is General Miletic, and there are the abbreviations standing for the person who drafted the document, NT, and MM is the person who typed the handwritten document drafted by the person under the initials NT.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, at the time, during this period of time when sometimes you were present for short time in the Main Staff, other times, most of the time you're not, did you ever come across any of these documents that you have seen here and also during your proofing session with the Prosecution, allegedly signed by Radivoje Miletic with the statement, "Standing in" for yourself? Did you come across those documents at the time? And if you did, did you ever raise the matter with then General Major Miletic at all? So two questions. I hope there is no objection from Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday or the day before yesterday, I said that my absence from the staff was from the 29th of May to the beginning of November, and that only on the 28th of July I came back in order to see General Zivanovic off. Upon my return to the Main Staff, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry to interrupt, General. We just had an important date misstatement which we should probably get straight before it gets --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- too much further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not -- it says 28 of July here in the transcript and that's not correct, because the witness said yesterday and the day before 19th and 20th of July. So that's to correct the statement. Otherwise, General, you may proceed. And thank you for the interruption Mr. -- intervention, sorry, Mr. McCloskey. Yes, go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday I stated that I had not read these reports. During my short stays in the Main Staff I did not read reports or any other documents. Usually General Miletic was duty-bound to inform me verbally or to brief me of the general situation on the front line so as to enable me to establish the facts. I did the same for General Mladic when he returned from somewhere. I did not read documents which were no longer topical. That's why I did not notice that until the moment Mr. McCloskey showed them to me in Banja Luka. And then I saw that all the documents bore that indication. I did not read the reports, especially not the reports that were sent to the Supreme Command, because they were the thing of the past. When you're in war you usually look at the present and the future rather than the past. You don't look back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In any case, you were the Chief of Staff of the VRS in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was the Chief of Staff, and I said that I was the Chief of Staff from the 12th of May 1992 to 23rd December 1996, 1.687 days in total.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Starting with June 1993, up to the end of the war, you were General Miletic's immediate superior, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the moment when he was appointed the chief of education and operations administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During the two days before your testimony before this Trial Chamber, the Prosecutor showed you a number of documents allegedly signed by General Miletic or where his name is indicated. Is it correct that among these documents you did not see a single document that you might call illegal or irregular, save for some minor administrative mistakes or omissions?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you are saying. I saw a document bearing my signature in the binder with yellow stickers. The document speaks about the appointment of Colonel Krstic as the person acting for the commander of the Drina Corps. I don't remember the name of that document. In my view, that document was illegal, irregular, against the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But nothing shows or indicates that that document had anything to do with General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is nothing in that document to indicate any such thing that would make me think that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'll move on to something else. Is it correct that General Miletic, in June 1995, could not issue orders to the commanders or other officers in corps and brigades?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke of that yesterday. None of us, save for the commander of the Main Staff, was able to issue executive orders to subordinate units, unless the commander has authorised one of us to deal with one segment of the front, like he, for instance, authorised me to handle operation Lukavac 93, the counterattack in Bihac and the defence against Croatian Operation Storm. Only in such situations did one of his assistants receive a command role but not for the VRS as a whole but only as relating to a certain area, one section of the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said the day before yesterday that while you were at the Main Staff, and when General Mladic was absent, in fact when you were in the headquarters of the Main Staff, assistant commanders reported to you. Is it correct that when you were in Western Bosnia and General Mladic was not at the headquarters of the Main Staff, assistant commanders did not report to General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They reported to the most senior general who happened to be around at the Main Staff. So if it was General Djukic or General Gvero, they reported to him. And of course, Miletic, as a figure who united and coordinated the work of the Main Staff, was always present. However, in view of the military chain of command and hierarchy, reports were received by one of the assistant commanders who happened to be there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said the day before yesterday that in your absence, General Miletic was not able to take over all your functions and, for instance, he was not sent on field trips to inspect units. Is it correct that in your absence, General Miletic was never deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Miletic was never deputy commander, or rather, he never stood in for the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And General Miletic did not have the powers to coordinate the work of assistant commanders?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he substituted for me, he had to coordinate the work of assistant commanders, but not in an order-issuing sense, but rather in an advisory role. I don't know which word to use. Perhaps the best word is a non-binding sense, as deputy Chief of Staff it was his duty to tell General Gvero, for instance, General Djukic in logistical units has a problem that your sector should deal with, for instance, crime, theft of materiel, or he would tell General Djukic, as chief of logistics, General Gvero has a problem with supplies in his sector, he has no paper, no pens, no speakers, no radio devices, no television sets, whatever he needed for security purposes. So he was the one who coordinated but not in the sense of issuing orders. That was something that General Mladic could do or I in Mladic's absence but he could tell Gvero, "Go to that logistical unit and check why there are so many violations and infractions, it's beginning to affect morale." Or he could tell Djukic, "Find those supplies and materiel." So he could not exactly speak in a commanding tone. He could tell others, this or that sector needs such and such supplies or assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Madam Fauveau. And he would do this without consulting you? Is that a proposition that you would accept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He would certainly do it without consulting me, because in order to consult me he would have had to establish contact with me across 600 or 700 kilometres, and there was no need for the enemy to be allowed to listen in on our conversations about Djukic needing pencils or some unit having a lot of offences, disciplinary infractions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if you had been present, in the same circumstances that you have just described, say needing to approach General Djukic or needing to approach General Gvero, would your intervention have been a command, an order, or would it still be an advice to either or both of the two generals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If General Mladic was at the Main Staff, then my role would be the same as the role I have described for Miletic a moment ago. I was also an assistant commander except that I was the first among equals in a way. However, if Mladic was not around, then I did have a command role. I could order Miletic or Djukic to give Gvero what he needed, such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just to clarify, I believe you've already mentioned it, but just for everything to be clear, concerning General Miletic, even when General Mladic was not at the Main Staff headquarters, his position was never one from which he could issue orders to an assistant commander?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was never in a position to issue orders to assistant commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- for interrupting you. So as I understand it, if General Mladic was not there but you were there, you would have been issuing orders? But if General Mladic was not there and you also were not there, who would be in a position to issue orders, for instance, in this case, to General Djukic and General Gvero? No one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. No one. In that case, General Miletic would have had to call me regardless of the distance, but if the case in question called for it, if it was an emergency, he would have called me or if Mladic was closer, he would have had to call Mladic so that one of us could issue appropriate orders. However, in practice, in the practice of the Main Staff, such situations never arose because, after all, the Main Staff was a harmonious whole. We had a good mutual understanding. And I can't imagine a situation in which General Gvero would refuse the advice of General Miletic, and I can't imagine any of the assistant commanders having any quarrel with what Miletic proposed. We just never experienced such incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You already said on a number of occasions that in July 1995, you were the Chief of Staff of the VRS, and at that time, General Miletic was not an acting Chief of Staff, he was not in that position.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And equally, despite certain documents that were signed by General Miletic as your representative, General Miletic did not represent you legally, he was not your legal representative, your legal substitute, in the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said a number of times that General Miletic substituted for me in performing day-to-day staff duties during my absences from the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But he never had all the powers that you disposed of when you were present at the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never had such powers, and I just said a moment ago that he was not in a position to command assistant commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said the day before yesterday that the work of General Miletic was important. Could we say that in times of war, in an army, all the tasks at all levels are important?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most important mission in a war is to keep the trench you are holding. So Miletic's trench was to design documents, to make plans, to coordinate the work of subordinated units, with a view to accomplishing the uniform task of all VRS units, and that is to defend Republika Srpska. Miletic did this as the officer -- an officer of the staff. The value of every operations officer is great, is crucial, but operations officers are considered to be the soul of an army. In this case, he was the soul of the Main Staff of the VRS. He knows everyone, he is able to advise everyone, to give them the appropriate information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to describe the tasks of General Miletic but to tell me if there is one kind of work or one mission or one task in an army, any army, that you could describe as not important.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said the day before yesterday that when you were at the Main Staff headquarters, it was a rare occurrence for Mladic not to accept your proposals. Could we say that General Mladic had a particular trust in you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, since he selected me to be his deputy and he never refused or significantly modified my proposals, and if I made any decisions in his absence, he never cancelled my decisions upon his return, which he had the right to do. On the contrary, he supported the execution of my decision. Sometimes he made minor changes but he never cancelled a single decision I made.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that the relations between General Mladic and General Miletic were not of the same nature as your relations with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean interpersonal relations?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: No. I mean work relations.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The working relationship of General Mladic to all members of the Main Staff were professional, although I have an idea of what you might be driving at. So tell me again, do you mean interpersonal relations?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If you wish, perhaps we can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when General Miletic came to the Main Staff, he was appointed to the administration from the artillery and rocket administration, which was not very busy because rocket systems of air defence were under the command of air defence and air force, and the rocket systems themselves were dispersed across units. So we started deploying Miletic on the front line, mainly around the Main Staff, units defending the Main Staff and some other units but mainly there in eastern Bosnia. And on one occasion, General Mladic was inspecting the front line close to the Main Staff. I believe it was on the side of Zepa. And I believe he yelled and hollered at Miletic, who was then Lieutenant Colonel, and when he returned to the Main Staff, he told me, "This bloke Miletic did not do anything. He could have but he didn't." But I knew the situation well myself and I realised that Miletic -- there was nothing Miletic could have done, and I told Mladic, "In my mind, Miletic is a good staff officer. He's a good officer. Let's not send him to the front any more. Let him rather help out here in the Main Staff." Because at that time, I had been alone in the staff sector for three or four months. Mladic did not say anything to that, but that was the last time that he gave Miletic any tasks on the front line himself. And since Miletic was a native of that area around Foca, I always took him with me when I visited that area because he knew the terrain well. At the beginning of the war, Mladic did not have much use for Miletic, and later on I did not have much insight into how their relation developed. I don't know about Miletic, but I know that Mladic did not have any great sympathy for Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And is it correct that General Miletic was never Mladic's adviser and certainly not his main adviser?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was certainly not his main man, but whether he ever provided any advice to Mladic, well, he probably did, sometimes when my functions were distributed to others in my absence. Then Miletic would suggest to Mladic how to use units, and advising the commander amounts to giving the commander your opinion how that should be done and Miletic could do that because he was the best-informed on the situation in various theatres of war in Republika Srpska, when I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You don't know to what extent General Mladic accepted Miletic's proposals?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was aware only of Mladic's executive decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we'll have the break now. How much more time do you require, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten to 15 minutes, I believe, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, Mr. Meek has joined us. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The day before yesterday you told us that in July 1995 the Supreme Commander, Radovan Karadzic, had started sending you orders directly, that they no longer went via General Mladic. Do you know whether Radovan Karadzic at the time sent orders directly to corps commanders as well?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st and the 2nd Corps of Krajina did not receive direct orders. I know that because I was in their zones of responsibility. I was the only one who received them. I don't know anything about the other corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The day before yesterday you spoke about the Lukavac operations-- operation, and you told us that that operation had been planned. The Lukavac operation, was it an operation by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to your information, the Krivaja operation that took place in July 1995 around Srebrenica was a spontaneous operation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the existence of any plan for that operation, so I would say that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In any case, based on your information, this was not an operation by the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, this operation was an operation of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were in Western Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just -- I think that's an incomplete answer to your question. "At the beginning, this operation was an operation of the Drina Corps," you said, General. And after the beginning, what was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what happened after the beginning. I don't know how General Mladic found himself in that part of the front. I suppose that he did it by design. And I don't know how this operation expanded, how it went on. I only know that at that time I suffered major losses in the western front and that on the -- from the Main Staff, I asked for reinforcement amounting to at least three brigades and every time, I got an answer that I could not count on such reinforcement because the troops were engaged in eastern Bosnia, i.e., on the eastern front. I was also told that I would receive the requested brigades once the burden was off that part of the front, and I indeed received them between the 1st and the 3rd August 1995, when it was already too late for me because by then I had already lost Grahovo and Glamoc and VRS started withdrawing from that part of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When General Miletic drafted regular reports, is it true that these reports featured the situation in the entire territory of Republika Srpska, in all of its front lines?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He received reports from the subordinate commanders. I've already spoken about that. And he simply conveyed two or three items from their reports. One of them was the situation on the front line, the situation on the territory, and the planned actions for the following day. He only united all these reports and conveyed them further.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But in order to draft his report, he had to read all the other reports, the reports of Drina Corps, the Sarajevo Corps, the 1st Corps, the 2nd Corps, the Eastern Bosnian Corps and the Herzegovina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. Yes. He had to do that regardless of whether he was to draft a report to the Supreme Command or not. He had to do it because he was an operations man.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As an operations man, he deemed all the front lines equally important, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that based on the function that he had in June 1995, General Miletic did not have any authority with regards to the prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think we have another date problem. Excuse me for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the transcript stands corrected. Instead of June 1995, it should be July 1995. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please repeat your question, Madam?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll repeat it to you myself. The proposition that was put to you is whether it is correct that based on General Miletic's functions in July 1995, he did not have any authority with regards to prisoners of war. Would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would. He did not have any authority. He was supposed to register the number of enemy imprisoned and also the number of our troops who were captured. There were other sectors that were in charge of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were in Western Bosnia, the information about the western Bosnian front line were included into the report to -- of the VRS Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I did not send the written combat reports to the Main Staff. This was done by the commanders of the 1st and the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But this was the area in which you performed your operations, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. This is the area where I was in charge of combat operations, but it had been agreed that I would not write combat reports. I only communicated orally with General Mladic. He would call me and then I would inform him about the situation on that front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General Miletic received information about the situation in Western Bosnia. Can we then say that General Miletic did not have any authority with regard to the operations that were carried out in Western Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can say that because General Miletic could not act as my commander. He could not issue me orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When it comes to the events around Srebrenica, can we say that General Miletic did not have any authority or influence on the activities that took place around Srebrenica and Zepa in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. McCloskey? He's answered the question but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that question is, especially given his precision definitions, vague. I think the question, if it was asked does he have any command authority, I think it's a fair question, but authority and his responsibilities I think have been clearly defined by the witness so I think we -- in order for this to be a proper question, it should say command authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I think -- my suggestion is that you take this up on recross -- re-examination, redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would agree that he has no command authority so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but he's also testified about General Miletic's and everyone else's advisory powers within the Main Staff, and that could fall under the question, under the aspect of influence, so you may take it up on redirect. Go ahead, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the witness has already answered my question. However, I would like to thank the witness, because I have no further questions. But I would also like to respond to the Prosecutor's objection. We are talking about the immediate superior of General Miletic, who is certainly well-suited to answer a question of that kind. And I don't have any further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, General. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was interrupted midway through my answer. I said no, he did not have any influence, and I wanted to add "in command sense," but I was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So do you wish to add anything to what you have just stated? Do you think your answer is now complete or do you wish to add on to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just added, "In command sense."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the witness's answer, with your leave I would like to clarify this answer. I would kindly ask you to allow me to put another question to the witness in order to clarify the previous answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, when were you in Western Bosnia, what kind of influence did General Miletic have on the operations in Western Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None whatsoever, in command sense again.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In what sense did he have influence?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, when I asked for the three brigades, he answered that the Main Staff could not send me those three brigades and he explained why. Also, if I approached the Main Staff in order to request additional materiel, ammunition, fuel and so on and so forth, he would convey my messages to the commander of the Main Staff on -- or the assistant commander for logistics or if I had problems with the state of morale, he would convey those as well. In other words, he was my intermediary in my communication with the other members of the Main Staff, and very often even with the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And just to clarify things further, the decision not to send brigades, ammunition, fuel, and other things that you mentioned to you, this was not General Miletic's decision, was it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. He only conveyed my requests to the commander and the commander's response to me in turn.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In other words, his influence or his responsibility was to convey what you had requested to somebody else and to make sure that the request was conveyed properly, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will put a question of my own on that, but in your absence, during the meetings of the Main Staff, if they happened to be discussing, for instance, the operation in Western Bosnia that you have been referred to, apart from any messages that he would pass on on your behalf, would -- was General Miletic in a position to contribute to the discussion with his own advice, independently of you and independently of any suggestions or proposals or messages that you might have conveyed to him earlier on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, he could participate in discussions, because he was standing in for me and he could convey proposals to the commander, just like me, because he was familiar with the corps reports, he was familiar with the situation based on my conversations with him, and he could explain the situation in Western Bosnia as well as I could have myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, General. Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Who is next? Have you discussed this amongst yourselves? Yes, Mr. Sarapa. Could you introduce yourself to the General, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General, my name is Djordje Sarapa, appearing for General Pandurevic. I phrased my questions, at least I tried, in such a way that most of them can be answered with a yes or no. Let me begin. The army of Republika Srpska was formed on the 12th of May 1992. Could you tell me if before that time, before the VRS was officially established, there had already been established military and paramilitary organisations of Muslims such as Green Berets, the Patriotic League, and others?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I mean Muslim military and paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was the Patriotic League, Green Berets, and some smaller, purely nationalist paramilitary groups called mosque pigeons, jihad warriors, swallows, larks. Those are the ones I can remember. THE TRANSLATOR: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you agree that by the decision to establish the army of Republika Srpska, only legal basis were given, only a legal basis was given for establishing the VRS, whereas the task of establishing actual units fell to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, if you have understood the question, then proceed to answer it. If you have not, you have every right to ask for a clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I understood. Before that decision of the 12th of May 1992 to establish the army, or, rather, that decision legalised what already existed, in terms of Serbs under arms, and the Main Staff was given the assignment to organise a real army and that was the 7th armed force on the territory of the former SFRY, because the prior six had already been established, some as long back as one year, others just a few months prior. The self-organisation of the Serbian people began already in end 1991, when the assembly, the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, fell apart. It was still called the assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with equal, if it was equal, representation of all ethnic groups in Bosnia, so that at the level of many municipalities, not all but many, brigades were formed. At the time they were called TO, Territorial Defence, brigades. Similarly, since it was people organising themselves, those were paramilitary units because they fell outside the official army that existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, that is the Yugoslav People's Army. There also existed certain armed groups, typical paramilitaries, that were organised on purely nationalist principles. With the establishment of the Main Staff, it was decided and it was one of our first decisions, that all those municipal units should be placed under the command of the Main Staff. It was decided to organise commands of corps, that all those nationalist paramilitaries, such as Arkan's Tigers, Mauzer's Panthers, a group called Repici, I can't remember all of them now, some Chetnik groups, of this or that political party, that all of them should be summoned and placed under the command of the army of Republika Srpska. Those who failed to comply were to be broken up, disbanded and expelled from our territory. With the exception of Arkan's Tigers and that group called Repici, all of them placed themselves under the command of the VRS. The tigers were expelled from the area around Bijeljina and Zvornik, while Repici were crushed a month or two later and their leader, as far as I know, was convicted and sentenced to 15 years in prison. And he died in Sremska Mitrovica, in prison. So some form of military organisation existed even before the official decision to set up the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you for that exhaustive answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, when did the formal presence of the JNA end in Republika Srpska? Was it before the coming into existence formally of the VRS or after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Eight days after the decision was made to establish the army of Republika Srpska, the JNA ceased to exist in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was supposed to pull out by 15 May. However, there was a delay and the last soldier of the JNA left Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 20th of June. We consider that 23rd June is the date of establishment of the VRS, when the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted the decision to call a general mobilisation of Serbian people in the territory of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us briefly, what were the main problems that were demonstrated in establishing the VRS, especially in terms of organisational, mobilisational readiness and combat readiness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take them one by one, please, General. Start with organisational problems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first organisational difficulty was due to the lack of capacity in the Ministry of Defence of the Serbian Republic to conduct the mobilisation. So this task was shifted to the Main Staff. For that reason we had to set up a special sector called the sector for mobilisation, reinforcement and personnel, and we somehow overcame that difficulty, because the -- there was already an awareness among the people that we had to go to war, that the war had been imposed on us, and we didn't have any problem with call-ups, save for some deserters who escaped to their back-up homeland, Serbia. Through the authorities in Serbia and Montenegro and through the Ministry of Defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and its General Staff, we interceded to have these deserters returned from the territory of Yugoslavia so that all officers, NCOs and civilians be returned from Yugoslavia, be turned back from Yugoslavia, if they were natives of Republika Srpska. Another problem we encountered was financial. We had a problem supplying the army with ammunition, weapons, fuel, uniforms, food, everything that the army needs. As far as food and clothing -- sorry, clothing and footwear were concerned, we kept what we had, what we were wearing, and taking the example of other armies that were formed after the break-up of the JNA, we also kept most of the materiel and equipment of the JNA that happened to be on the territory of Republika Srpska when the JNA left, starting with depots of weapons and ammunition, reserves of fuel and even reserves of clothing and footwear, anything that was already on our territory. So that when the JNA left Bosnia and Herzegovina, regardless from which territory and regardless from -- regardless of which group controlled the particular territory, the JNA could only pull out its soldiers and the weapons that they were carrying. It was not that easy to keep those JNA resources but we managed because we were the last armed force to be formed in the Balkans, and we always invoked that when the Slovenes seized things from us or Croats robbed us of the entire Varazdin Corps, we said we are entitled to keep the materiel. The next problem was the problem of command in the army. We inherited the structure of command over the corps that happened to be in the territory of Republika Srpska. Mr. President, I don't think it would be advisable for me to, explain now how each of the corps command came into being. At any rate, the numbers of those corps commands --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you explained enough. I would suggest you go to the mobilisation problems, if you had any, and finally combat readiness. These are the other two aspects that Mr. Sarapa asked you about. When the VRS was -- came into being, did it have any particular mobilisation problems that you are aware of? If not, could you try and be brief in your answer so that we do our best to finish with your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said something about the staffing problems. Those were desertion of conscripts to Serbia or people who were hiding in the territory of Republika Srpska. We had no other problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So then let's move to combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't have almost any problems with combat readiness either because our officers were well trained. Five generals happened to be in the VRS there and four generals in the Main Staff, and two of us had completed all military schools, including the school of warfare. We had a sufficient number of highly educated Colonels, Lieutenant Colonels, and candidates for brigade commanders. Most of them had graduated from schools of warfare or tactical schools, unlike other ad hoc armies who had so-called artificial generals, as I called them. That applied to Croats and also Muslims, whose high-ranking officers had been the opposition or deserters in the former JNA. Unlike them, our senior staff was well trained. Those soldiers who happened to be serving their military service in the JNA at the time when the VRS was established just continued on, if they were natives of that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough, unless Mr. Sarapa disagrees. If you don't disagree could you proceed with your next question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. I believe that the answer was quite extensive and I will move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: General, you spent a number of years in the JNA as a high ranking officer and you're familiar with the structure of the army and the relationship between the army and the state organs in the former Yugoslavia. Also as the Chief of Staff of the VRS, of the Main Staff, you were also familiar with the situation in Republika Srpska and for that reason I believe that my next few questions will be easy for you to answer. Is it true that in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, as it used to be called, the General Staff of the JNA was an integral part of the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Is it also correct that in Republika Srpska, the Main Staff of the VRS was a state institution which was not part of the Ministry of Defence. Rather, it was subordinated directly to the President of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not part of the Ministry of Defence -- I explained that yesterday -- because none of us were members of the Supreme Command. We were subordinated directly to the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us that within the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, there was a sector for intelligence and security and that there were two administrations within that sector, the intelligence administration and the security administration. My next question with regard to this is as follows: Do you remember that the security administration in the former Yugoslavia was organised differently, that it was part of the Ministry of Defence, whereas the intelligence administration was part of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was the case. On the eve of the war, or immediately before I was sent out of Macedonia, I know that a decree had arrived about the unification of these two administrations and the creation of the intelligence and security administration. And I know when we established the Main Staff, a sector was established encompassing both these administrations, the intelligence and the security administrations. In other words, we adopted a last directive of the JNA about the organisation of these two administrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can we then say that the chief of the intelligence administration --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- was the assistant Minister of Defence whereas the intelligence administration chief was the assistant commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't answer this question because while I was in the JNA, this was much too high for me. I just carried orders of the army commander and lower-ranking officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Can we then say that the Main Staff of the VRS army was directly linked to the corps and independent units?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I was bragging about that and saying that I could -- had to push a button.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And the corps, did they have brigades and independent battalions linked to them?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but the links were not as automatic as they were at the higher level, between the General Staff and the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: At the level of the Main Staff, you established teams of officers who controlled the situation in the unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have inspection for combat readiness like armies normally have. We had ad hoc teams or groups which we would send to the units in order to establish the level of their combat readiness and the situation on the front lines in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Did the corps commands do the same with regard to the lower units, for example brigades?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They adopted the same principle and they used the same system as the system that the Main Staff applied with regard to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: The officers who inspected the commands and units, did they have their team leaders? In other words, was anybody of them in charge? Did anybody of them act as the first among the equals?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The team leaders were well known. If the team was sent to the corps, then it would be General Mladic who would head the team, or myself, or one of their assistants, depending on what the focus of the inspection was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: In such cases, the commander of the Main Staff, i.e., the corps commander, if the team was sent from the corps, could they authorise the team leader or one of the officers to influence the situation in the lower units on the spot?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could, and they did, regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can we say that the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS army was an undisputable authority?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was an undisputable authority in the armed forces, and he also had authority among the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Is it also correct that the officers from the Main Staff were also respected by the lower-ranking commands and officers?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure that in my case that was the case. I don't know about the others, how they were perceived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: You personally inspected corps commands and lower units during the war and you spent a lot of time on the ground observing combat operations, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any cases of an officer from the Main Staff issuing orders to brigade commanders and that the corps commander were not informed about such an order that had been issued?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should not have happened. If it did happen, the officer who did that would be taken to task for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Are you aware of any such cases? Are you familiar with any of them?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there were one or two such cases. They were done by Colonel Zivanovic, the chief of artillery. He was familiar with Podrinje, and the commander would often send him to inspect the area from Zvornik to Foca. On one occasion the commander of the 1st Bircani Brigade Svetozar Andric, complained about Zivanovic. Zivanovic had supposedly entered the brigade and issued orders about the redeployment of a battalion, and I believe that there was another such case in the Visegrad Brigade. The commander at the time was Vinko Pandurevic. Zivanovic also issued certain orders to that brigade, but around that time, Zivanovic was seriously wounded and for that reason no measures, no disciplinary measures, were taken against him. I don't know about any other cases. We had 143 units at the level of either a regiment or brigade so I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your answer was quite detailed. Is it true that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Sarapa. Mr. McCloskey?
