utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: May be helpful if we could just clear up which Zivanovic this is and what his particular position was. People may be confused about that as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think the message is clear. It's in your hands, Mr. Sarapa, or if the general wishes to proceed by clarifying this, he may do so, without your intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the general understands the intervention and that he will be able to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name is Milenko Zivanovic. When he arrived from Benkovac, he was appointed the chief of artillery in the Main Staff, during the formation of the Drina Corps, as the 6th Corps of the VRS army, and this took place on the 1st November, when he was discharged from the hospital, Milenko Zivanovic was appointed commander of that corps. In other words, this was Milenko Zivanovic, the future commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Is it true that rules and regulations provide a certain rank and position for every position in the army?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what is a position group?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A position group determined the salary. For example, two lieutenant colonels, one would be a brigade commander and the other would be an administrative officer in a command or in a staff. The Lieutenant Colonel who acts as a brigade commander would have a higher pay than the Lieutenant Colonel who works in a staff and who doesn't have any responsibility for the personnel. A PG, position group -- a PG stands for position group but popularly it was also known as a pay group amongst us officers or a pay grade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could we also say that a position group also denoted the duties, the level of duties, of an officer?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Was it common, was it a common practice, that officers were appointed to certain positions, to certain formations, not having the required ranks? In other words, their ranks were lower than were required by a certain formation or position group?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republika Srpska army did have such a situation. The commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, General Momir Talic, was a higher ranking officer than me and he was also older than me. For example, in 1993, he was Lieutenant General, and I was a General Major. However, my PG, i.e., my function, was higher than his. Still, I never arrived in the area of his corps's responsibility without General Momir Talic reporting to me at the entrance into his area of responsibility, into the area of responsibility of his corps. In the eyes of the people who attended this act, this looked strange. They wondered how it was possible for a higher ranking officer to report to the General Major. Still, this was in keeping with the rules and General Talic never violated that obligation that he had towards me, whereas he did violate that obligation towards General Mladic, and he accounted for that in the following words: "If I don't report to Milovanovic, I will jeopardise his authority in the army, and if I don't report to Mladic, I do not jeopardise Mladic's authority because Mladic can punish me for that whereas Milovanovic does not have that possibility." We avoided situations in which we would have such things happening in the lower-ranking units. We had a staffing problem a few months into the war. It was very difficult to find commanders for the three corps, the Sarajevo, the Herzegovina and the Eastern Bosnian Corps, and we were forced to appoint one of the most capable commanders of one of the brigades for the commander of the east corps. At that time he was a colonel, Novica Simic. He remained bearing that rank for only two or three months. He took over that duty in the corps where there were some older colonels who were close to retirement. The problem was solved very quickly. The older colonels were sent to retirement or they were sent to some other units, and very soon, the Eastern Bosnia Corps was regenerated so to speak, and all the officers were of a younger generation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Were there cases that you were familiar with that brigade commanders were captains or majors, although they should have been colonels or high-ranking officers?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, that was a very common occurrence, I dare say. Lieutenant colonels and colonels, Serbs and Montenegrins, withdrew together with the JNA and we were left with the lower-ranking officers. For example, the commander of the Protection Regiment, Colonel Suput left with the JNA and the oldest officer in the Protection Regiment was Captain First Class Milomir Savcic, and he was appointed the commander of the regiment. Throughout the war he remained in that position as the regiment commander. And at the end of the war he was promoted and became a colonel and after the war, he was even promoted to the rank of a general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa, I hate to interrupt you. You know that we very rarely do that, but what's the relevance of this? Can't we go straight to what is really relevant to your case? I mean, if you can explain the relevance, of course we can live up with all these questions and long answers, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll move on to other questions. But as for this one, it was asked because General Pandurevic at the time when he was appointed commander of the Zvornik Brigade, had the rank of Captain First Class, and the idea of my question was to establish what the situation was like generally and in what position he himself was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's clear enough. Now I suggest you proceed to more substantive matters. Thank you, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Regarding the rules in the army of Republika Srpska, you wrote in your book covering the issues of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that you had taken the rules of the former JNA and adapted them. Does that particularly apply to rules governing brigades?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I spoke of that yesterday. We didn't adapt our rules to the rules of the JNA. On the contrary, we adapted the rules of the JNA to our own needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Were there any planned announced controls and inspections of subordinate units by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Were there any unannounced controls?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Does that apply to checks made by the Main Staff but also corps commands?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unannounced checks were made by General Mladic or I, upon his orders. If any other people came to inspect units, such as team leaders, their visits would be announced. I believe the same is true of corps commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: In addition to usual inspections of units, were there also inspections by chiefs of sectors?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they had to ask for permission to do that, from the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could the same be said of individual inspections by officers from a corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, because the Chief of Staff of a corps, if he wants to leave the command of the corps, has to require permission from his commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: In such cases, these senior officers from superior commands, do they have to report to the brigade commander, let him know they have arrived?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We've already discussed this when we talked of Milenko Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: In the case of such a visit, would the brigade command be required to provide all the necessary conditions for unhindered work of such a visitor from a superior command?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a brigade commander never knows whether the officer from the Main Staff came announced or unannounced, whether it was a planned inspection or an unplanned one. However, the brigade commander is required to inform immediately the corps commander of such a visit, and the corps commander knows whether the visit had been announced or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: In such a case, would the brigade commander be required to provide all the facilities to that visitor who came to inspect?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So if we are talking specifically about a brigade, would he be required to act in that way regardless of whether the inspector was coming from the Main Staff or from the corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: You personally frequently passed through Zvornik, and you stopped by the command of the Zvornik Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: On such occasions, would the commander report to you about the situation within the brigade, practically in the absence of anybody else from the command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I required them to do so, yes, he would report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. Through a combination of circumstances you were aware of the situation in the Zvornik Brigade, perhaps better than in other brigades. Do you know that at the beginning of the war in Zvornik, the Zvornik Brigade had quite a lot of problems?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had a lot of problems selecting the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you know that a lot of commanders of the Zvornik Brigade came and went?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Vinko Pandurevic was the third or the fourth brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you remember that even parts of the 65th Protection Regiment were engaged to deal with certain problems that had resulted from the presence of paramilitaries and the poor discipline within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that one unit from the regiment was engaged, whether the battalion of the military police or the sabotage detachment, to break up this paramilitary unit called Repici that consisted of about 70 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Are you aware that after brigade commander Major Petkovic, Dragan, was wounded in October 1992, there was a problem appointing the new commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I mentioned that Vinko Pandurevic was the third or the fourth, I had forgotten about Petkovic, although I know all about the incident in which he was wounded and indeed there was a problem appointing the new commander because municipal authorities considered that brigade to be their own property and they tried to impose a commander of their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: You do know, don't you, that in December 1992, Vinko Pandurevic became commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he did, but I take your word for it being in October [as translated].

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you know that he was very young at the time, only 32 years old, and that he had the rank of Captain First Class?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew all that, and I knew that Vinko Pandurevic had before that successfully organised the Visegrad Brigade and he was successful in fighting in middle Podrinje and as far as I remember, it was I who suggested Vinko Pandurevic to be appointed commander of the Zvornik Brigade to overcome all the problems that existed, including political ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you remember that due to his efforts to organise the brigade along military principles, he came into conflict with municipal authorities very soon after his appointment?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa, just for clarification, line 13, should it not be 37 years old -- age?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 32, 32. He was 32 years old at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he was appointed brigade commander in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, he couldn't have been a Captain First Class at age 32. If he had completed the military academy, he had to be -- he had only nine years to change four ranks. You have to hold one rank for at least three years. In fact, never mind, I'm not really interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: According to our records, he was born on the 25th of June of 1959 and if we are talking of an appointment in 1992, I forget exactly which month --

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 33 years, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That solves the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show Exhibit 7D460? Just a little lower, please, so we can see the top of the document. It's all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: General, please look at this regular combat report, daily combat report, dated 23rd of February 1993. It's addressed to you personally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that's correct. I don't see February. I see 23 and 1993 but I believe you. Never mind that it's February.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can we see page 3 of this document? Could you please look at the signature?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can we see page 2 now? Mr. Milovanovic, could you please read paragraph 3, status of morale and security? Just the first one.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Due to undue haste and the public character of the decision to establish the manoeuvring brigade, and designating its commander in advance, as well as the attempt to bring back the old brigade commander through the back door without any formal legal basis, and as a result of unlawfully designating persons substituting for the commander in his absence on private errands, we are facing a double" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel be asked to stop so that we can actually interpret this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We are facing the phenomenon of duplicated or double command and control, the spreading of rumours, divisions among members of the units or rifts among troops, denigration of the Chief of Staff, (the lawful deputy commander, which the said person has in no way deserved; on the contrary), which significantly contributed to the current sentiment within the unit and its combat readiness."

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you please continue reading? Can you please read the second passage?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be instructed to read slowly, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In the interests of maintaining the high level of morale and combat readiness of the brigade, irrespective of individual credits, interests, in the ranks of politics and the army, it is necessary to honour the prevalent rules and regulations at all levels. Hereby request that the corps commander clearly informs the organs in the municipality as well as the planned new commander who the commander is and what -- and on what basis and who holds the responsibility in the brigade in order to avoid duplication, which is very" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you stop for a moment for the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: --"to avoid duplication, which is very dangerous for the system of command and control in the brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you please continue?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In order to avoid duplication, which is very dangerous in the process of command and control. On my own behalf, I shall try to prevent this with all means and very energetically because I believe that this phenomenon has been caused for the most part by the premature public information, information for the general public, of the decision of the corps commander upon the proposal of the president of the municipality. By that act, the command and control over the army has been brought into a rather [unintelligible] position. I expect from the corps commander to protect the process of command and control and his subordinates and to do so by helping the work of the brigade commander whose work has maintained the situation under control. "The regular and planned tasks as well as extraordinary tasks of sending 150 troops to the 2nd Motorised Romanija Brigade are being carried out. In the territory there is an attempt to undermine the work of the brigade commander, by instigating dissatisfaction among the troops. This is done by the official institutions of the municipality and also by some vain individuals. The climate that has been created in the territory and the way the official organs and institutions in the municipality work are aimed at recruiting commanders and officers for their own interests, and when this fails, in case of responsible and principled commanders who tries at all costs to protect the unit and maintain a high level of combat readiness, they are trying to deal with such a commander using even the dirtiest methods. The highest number of officers of the brigade commanders and the battalion commanders condemn such practices very strongly, and they give full support to the brigade commander." Sir, I really don't understand why you made me read this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation, Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Yes, I have, yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise, the general will go home unhappy. Let's please try to finish with his testimony today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember this situation which was present in Zvornik at the time of this report?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a computer. There is no way for me to remember this particular report, but I do remember the situation, and I also remember that between the brigade commander, Pandurevic, and the corps commander, Milenko Zivanovic, there were always harsh words said, and there were always misgivings and misunderstandings. Vinko was an educated man. You see in his signature, the title, master of arts or sciences, which could not be said of General Zivanovic. He did finish some military schools but he did not have much of a general education. The only thing he knew was cannons and howitzers. I know when this telegram arrived, General Mladic called the president of the municipality of Zvornik, Branko Djuric, if I'm not mistaken about the name. What Mladic told him, I don't know. They -- the two of them spoke. But I know that after that, Vinko no longer had any problems with the municipal authorities. I know that currently, Djuric is in prison in Belgrade, where he's being held responsible for some crimes committed during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you remember that Pandurevic was denied the fact that he was trained in the military school and the school of national defence?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only Pandurevic, but all the officers who developed to the level of being entitled to such education, because of the war, this was also denied to Novica Simic, the commander of the East Bosnia Corps. We managed to send them to Yugoslavia where we educated our staff. The cutoff age for war school was 42 but this did not apply to the members of the army of Republika Srpska. We managed to agree with the schools in Yugoslavia that we would send them for education once the war was over irrespective of their age at the time. And Vinko was enabled to get his Ph.D. while serving in the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: When I put my question to you, and when I mentioned the school of national defence, he was denied education in 1997, when the war was already over, if you remember that.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to insult you but you were supposed to listen to me yesterday. In 1996, I was removed from my position, not just me but the whole of the Main Staff and up to 1998 I did not hold any functions, I did not hold any positions, and in 1998 I was appointed a Minister of Defence so I really don't have a clue why his education was denied, who denied it or anything to -- of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown Exhibit P02509? The document has been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it a quick question and answer, Mr. Sarapa? Because within two minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I now see that the time is -- has come for the break so maybe it would be best if we had our break now and then I'll proceed after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much time do you require, Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, before the end of today, I will finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the position -- thank you, Mr. Sarapa. What's the position with regard to the Beara team and the Nikolic team?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have very few questions, if any. We are still just consulting, so we will be limited -- reduced from what we told the Court yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. On the basis of what we heard, we will require 15 minutes with this witness but not more than 15 minutes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I suggest you consult a little bit with each other to see whether you can then finish with Simic tomorrow, because if it's unlikely, then I would prefer not to have him here, I mean, because it would mean interrupting his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We can definitely finish with Simic if we start him tomorrow morning. I've spoken to my colleagues who I think have the most interest and I think in fact he will be able to to be completed probably in the first session for sure, in a session. We can talk after the break. But that does bring up the issue Your Honour raised earlier about the next witness and the motion to add some exhibits to the 65 ter list. We didn't think we were going to reach him but now it looks possible, if not likely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then if that's the case, we will require a response from the Defence, but we acted before on the statement of Mr. McCloskey that that was not likely to be the case tomorrow. So we'll -- please, do have some mutual consultations during the next 25 minutes when we will have the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you come to an accord as to how we are going to proceed? Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've added up some of the time and I may have 30 minutes, but if we are lucky we'll finish tomorrow morning with the witness. Maybe tonight. It wasn't clear to me the estimate from the Defence but I'm told Mr. Sarapa has no more questions so we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's to disagree with Mr. McCloskey, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. This was actually decided even before we heard from Mr. McCloskey. I would have more questions but I don't have the time. I have a question about document P02509 but it doesn't have to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: This is my last question, General. Do you remember that one of the brigades that at the beginning of August 1995 arrived in Krajina was a brigade from the Drina Corps under the command of Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this very well. It arrived on the 3rd of August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this answer and for all the others, and I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I actually go home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is next, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My name is Stephane Bourgon and I represent the accused Drago Nikolic in this case and I have just a few questions for you so I believe that indeed you should be able to go home today. Firstly, General, I'd like you to confirm, this is something that you already referred to in your testimony, that the VRS inherited from the JNA the doctrine that guided its actions during the war. I'm not talking about the rules. I'm talking about the doctrine. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A doctrine is something else. And combat rules are a different thing. A doctrine is a political position of the state with regard to defence, whereas combat rules are combat rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But would I be right in saying that what guided the actions of the VRS during the war, you inherited for the most part from the JNA even though you adapted it to suit your own needs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that is correct is that we adopted combat rules, i.e., provisions of the combat rules, from the JNA. Everything else, i.e., the higher forms of defence, were adapted to the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, within those combat rules that you say you adopted, would I be right in saying that the conduct of military activities was divided between the strategic, the operational and the tactical level?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And of course, when we speak about the Supreme Command, then we are talking about a body that operates at the strategic level; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Supreme Command and the Main Staff are strategic commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my next question, in terms of you yourself, in your capacity as Chief of Staff of the Main Staff, you also worked at the strategic level but of course, the Main Staff has some responsibility for overseeing operational level activities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The operative level of activities belongs to the corps and their zones, and as for the tactical level -- and I'm anticipating your next question -- are brigades and lower ranking units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, general. That was exactly my next question, that brigades operate indeed at the tactical level. Now, the fact that a brigade works at this level, I'm talking about the tactical level, would I be right in saying that this implies that a brigade is given and expected to accomplish specific tasks which somehow fit in into the overall strategic plan issued by the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: The ensemble of technical actions is the operative level. If two or more corps prefer one task, this is strategic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It may be my question was not precise enough. If we are talking about the brigade, at the tactical level, would I be right in saying that a brigade will be issued some specific tasks and is expected to execute and accomplish these specific tasks? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A brigade is given precise tasks with regard to the space, time and level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like you to simply have a quick look at Exhibit P2755, if we can call this up on the e-court, please. You are familiar with this document, General, and I'd simply like you to confirm that this is an example of a strategic-level document. And I refer you specifically to where it says "the strategic objectives of the Serbian people." So would I be right in saying that this is a strategic-level document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is a doctrine document. This has to do with the defence policy, and every item from 1 through 6 are strategic tasks for the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now my question is that if I look at these what you call strategic tasks being given to the army of Republika Srpska, would I be right in saying that brigades have no input regarding the adoption and/or drafting of such a document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only brigades, but also the corps and the Main Staff do not have any impact on this document. Not even the Supreme Command has any influence because there is a decision by the assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to move on now to another exhibit which is Exhibit P5, and I believe you are also familiar with this exhibit, if we can call this on the e-court, please, and, General, I'd like you to confirm that this exhibit that will appear before you is an example of a document which is prepared and issued at the strategic level, although it is addressed to the corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. This is okay. This is directive number 7. It could be understood as a document at the strategic level and the doctrine level. This concerns the defence policy, but some operative tasks are being defined so we can say that we are talking about the operative level as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this document, as you probably know, is signed by the Supreme Commander or Mr. Karadzic, and this document is dated on the 8th of March. Would I be right in saying that this document illustrates how, as of 8 March 1995, the strategic objectives of the Republika Srpska are to be accomplished by the corps of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff or the armed force as a whole performs strategic goals and since the tasks are divided by the corps, they perform operative tasks each in their respective area. Let me not go into what each corps did at that given time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Fully agree with you. I don't want you to go into what each of the corps was asked to do, simply to -- I'm talking about the nature and the character of the document, and my next question is: Can you confirm that this type of document, that once again brigades have no input or say regarding the adoption and/or drafting of such documents?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They did not have any input or say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question, General, and I think I have only two or three more questions and that will be it. You testified during the last two days concerning the duties, responsibilities and the authority of assistant commanders, of persons holding the position of assistant commanders within the Main Staff. I'd simply ask you to confirm that you would agree this also applies, albeit at a much lower level, to assistant commanders at the brigade level?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The structure of the brigade command differs greatly from the structure of the Main Staff and the corps command. Everything is at a smaller scale but the principles remain the same. The main decisions at the brigade level are made by the brigade commander. His deputy, i.e., Chief of Staff, has almost the same functions as I had in the Main Staff. He doesn't have different sectors but he has assistants for morale and for logistics and that would be that. In other words, the principle of work is the same, only at a somewhat smaller scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question refers to a question which was posed to you by my colleague representing the accused Pandurevic and that was at page 44, lines 1 to 5, of the transcript of today. Now, this question dealt with the inspections which may be conducted at lower levels than the corps. Now, I'll just read you the exact words which were mentioned and it goes as follows: "If the team was sent from the corps, could they authorise the team leader or one of the officers to influence the situation in the lower units on the spot?" And your answer to this question was, "Yes, they could, and they did, regularly." Now my question is simply, would you agree with me that when we talk about influencing the situation on the spot, that does not mean the authority to command the lower units? So this is not in the command sense. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. It could also be in the command sense because the team is sent and when the team is sent no matter from which level to a lower level it goes there not only to establish the situation but also to remove deficiencies and in order to remove deficiencies they have to be able to issue orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when that team issues orders, if you -- what kind of orders would that be? Orders to improve the operational effectiveness of the unit or actually combat orders? Would there be a distinction between the two?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the difference. If an inspecting body established that the brigade or one of its battalions is not properly deployed, that its tactical position is not good, the team leader has the powers to order the battalion to move immediately or to give them a certain deadline to move, forward, backward, left, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we take that not in the context of an inspection visit but simply in the context of an assistant commander coming from a higher level and visiting the brigade, you would agree with me that such an assistant commander cannot issue an order to that brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with you. It depends on what assignment that assistant commander received when he is going to inspect units on the front line. His assignment could be only to size up the situation and inform the commander upon his return. Another possibility is that he receives an assignment to redress the situation. In that case, he must have powers to issue orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then of course, General, he would deal with the commander of the unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, he would pass his orders through the unit commander. For instance, General Milovanovic would not just show up and move the battalion. He would take Vinko Pandurevic, the commander, aside, tell him what needs -- what he needs to tell him and then Vinko Pandurevic would be the one giving the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have one last question and this one is based on your experience as Chief of Staff, and I would ask you to -- I'd like to give you a situation and ask you for your -- based on your experience as Chief of Staff and your military experience. If I had a brigade Chief of Staff who is standing in as brigade commander, who is told by one of his -- one of the assistant commanders within the brigade that he has been given an order directly by Mladic, would it be normal for this Chief of Staff to act upon this order without verifying whether indeed it had been issued?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That hypothetical does not fairly reflect the facts of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we can discuss this in the presence of the witness in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, given that is my objection, I will then withdraw it as long as it's -- my position is known to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you wish to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, whether or not it matches the facts of this case is a matter for argument at a later time. I'm asking a question to the general. He was a Chief of Staff of the Main Staff. He is in a good position to answer how a chief of staff would react.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And he can just tell us if it's normal for a Chief of Staff to be told.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I will say my question again just to try to make it simple. The Chief of Staff at the brigade level who is standing in for his commander at the time, and he is told by one of his -- well, one of the assistant commanders that he has received an order directly from higher level, would it be normal for that Chief of Staff to accomplish that order or to give effect to that order without first checking or verifying whether such an order had indeed been issued?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the army, we are prone to say, first execute, then complain. So that Chief of Staff has the obligation to carry out the order and inform his immediate superior that he did it. So there is no delay in executing orders, especially in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I fully understand that war is a very -- represents very special circumstances but indeed you would agree that the Chief of Staff in such a situation would have at the first available opportunity to inform his superior of that situation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But informing the immediate superior must not delay the execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what if, General, this order that we are talking about involves the commission of a crime? Does that change the scenario around? Would he execute the order or would he first inform his superiors?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, must I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think unless you have reason that by answering this question, you might incriminate yourself, you are duty-bound to answer it because we have not stopped the question or asked you not to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, every officer has enough training and education to decide what is wrong and what is right. So it depends on the personality whether a specific person would carry out such an order or not. I personally wouldn't. You could see in directive 7/1 that a commander of the Main Staff did not transmit to the units that part of the directive number 7 which speaks of entering the enclaves, Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde. Therefore, General Mladic practically, in his order, refused or denied the order of the superior commander to enter the enclaves. That's at least what it looks like on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Just to make the situation clear, because I want to make sure that we are answering the same question, the Chief of Staff was told this not by assistant commander from the corps but he was told this from one of the brigade assistant commanders. Would he first immediately contact his superior before acting upon such an order? Would that be what military both customs and the rules call for?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A smart Chief of Staff would do exactly that. When he receives an order, he would first inform his immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. I take it that there are no other Defence teams that wish to cross-examine the witness. Do you have redirect, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Following on Mr. Bourgon's questions, would a smart Chief of Staff in this situation that he gave you, that had a trusted, for example, chief of security, if he'd asked his chief of security when he hears about this order from his chief, when he asked the chief, we've got to check with our commander about that and the chief says our commander knows about it, it comes from the highest, would that Chief of Staff normally trust his -- the word of his chief of security?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A smart one wouldn't. He would address his own commander, because the security chief is not superior to the Chief of Staff. On the contrary, in some cases, it is quite the opposite. Chief of Staff is a senior position. So he cannot ask a lower positioned person for approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, he wouldn't be asking him he would -- in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe my colleague should add, because if he's going to follow up on my question, he should say that at that moment the Chief of Staff is standing in for the commander of the brigade. That's very important. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I thought I had meant to adopt Mr. Bourgon's full question so he would have been the deputy commander actually of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I agree that that wouldn't be very smart just to go on the word of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But don't you have to -- or excuse me, your chief of security. In many contacts, especially in war, don't the commanders have to trust their subordinates, especially their chief of security?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon. One moment, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, the question is incomplete, do you trust your subordinate who tell to you accomplish a crime? That's very different. He's not giving all the exact question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree with Mr. Bourgon. I don't want to repeat the whole thing again, but I agree with him. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we all know which context we are talking about. So -- and the General too. He's heard the exchange and he can now proceed to answer the question. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon, and thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This exchange between counsel clarified the issue for me a little bit. We are talking about the Chief of Staff who is standing in for the brigade commander. In that case, his immediate superior is the corps commander and he would address the corps commander and inform him of the order he had received. He doesn't even need to ask the question, "Shall I execute or not," because it's obvious that a war crime is in question. It is the duty and the responsibility of the corps commander, that's why he was trained and appointed to that position, to say to him, "Carry it out or don't carry it out," if he is the same sort of person as the one who ordered the commission of a war crime in the first place. The difference is that I had understood Mr. Bourgon as saying that this person was a Chief of Staff acting in his own position rather than standing in for the brigade commander. Actually, he is functioning as the brigade commander and his first immediate superior in that case is the corps commander and there is absolutely no dilemma here. There is another situation involving an order that shouldn't be executed or wouldn't be executed. That is when executing an order poses a risk of material damage. For instance, a truck has a carrying capacity of 16 tonnes, and somebody orders that the truck be loaded with 20 tonnes. The truck can be destroyed. In that case, you don't execute the verbal order. You ask for an order in writing. It's the same thing in wartime. If somebody verges on unlawful action or possible war crime, you don't execute the order immediately, if it's verbal. You ask for that order in writing. In this way, the responsibility does not lie on the person executing. It moves to the person who issued the order. And that latter person is also protected in a certain way by having the order in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You talked a bit about the obligation that an officer has when he receives an order or a direction from a superior, that it was his obligation to do what he was told. I think you said that in the connection when General Miletic received directions in drafting directive 7. Now, had General Miletic received directions or orders from a superior in the drafting of directive 7 that were illegal, would he have had any duty to draft those illegal orders in the directive? Under the JNA rules and the rules the VRS we are working under.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, when General Miletic received such guidelines from the Supreme Commander, he had to inform General Mladic and ask for his permission or approval to do that because while doing that he was absent from the Main Staff and it would have been normal to inform General Mladic of the guidelines. But neither Mladic nor Miletic can influence the guidelines as such. The commander of the Main Staff can influence it, which he did with his own order. He deleted or omitted some clauses from that directive, risking court martial and God knows what other consequences, because he could have been tried for not strictly executing the orders of the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Miletic gets an illegal orders from President Karadzic and that illegal order is backed up by General Mladic. Is that a defence to General Miletic if he places that illegal order in the directive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I see Madam Fauveau. Doesn't that become an argument later on, Mr. McCloskey? Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if a clear answer can be given, no problem. If it's not a clear answer, I'll go to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe the Prosecutor is misstating the evidence and the facts, that General Miletic received orders to write something. Writing something is not illegal in itself. It remains to be seen what actually happened to that directive later and we saw what happened in view of what General Mladic did, but the order to write something cannot be regarded as an illegal order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to pursue the question, Mr. McCloskey, or shall we proceed to the next one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would of course adamantly disagree with her argument. That's a legal argument, and given that's the situation maybe we should just proceed to the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are proceeding to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, let's go to a document, it's 65 ter number 28. It's not one that I've -- I don't think I've shown you before. You may have seen it or not. It's, as we are waiting for it, hopefully the B/C/S will come up on your screen. It's entitled, "Main Staff of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska, military Prosecutor's Office at the Main Staff of the armed forces, guidelines for the determining criteria for criminal Prosecution." And it's dated 1992. I have a hard copy that -- it's coming but it will be easier for the general, I think, if he has something in his hands. Thank you, General, if you could just flip through that a bit see if you remember it. I know this is a while back. I'm particularly interested in section number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, a number of us are discussing this. We would quite like to know where Mr. McCloskey is going. I don't know whether he's prepared to indicate before he asks the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are talking about the duty to pass on orders regarding criminal offences, and this is the guideline to criminal offences, just asking him if it was in effect at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. We'll proceed unless we hear --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, if he's going to go ahead, can we all see the section on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's not in English or in B/C/S at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it does exist in B/C/S. And it exists also in English. Which part is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The part I wanted to ask the general about was section 3 entitled "Criminal offences against humanity and international law pursuant to chapter 16 of the Criminal Code." It's page 7 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I object to this kind of question if we are trying to finish today with this witness. This is beyond the scope of what was asked. I don't know where -- this document was not on the list that was given to us. It's a new document. And I don't know what kind of questions he wants to ask. I could wait for the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's wait for the question first and then see afterwards. It may become a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just do you recognise this document? Was it in effect at the time, General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognise the document and I don't know whether it was in force but I'm glad it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think that settles that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think so. Storm in a tea cup.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you've also spoken at some length about the various positions at the Main Staff and, in particular, you were asked questions about Gvero and Miletic. And I have a couple of documents from our time period that actually have their names in it and I think, if we could get your comments on that it would help us identify whether or not it fits the descriptions that you told us about their jobs. The first document I would go to is 65 ter number 33 and -- excuse me a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And this document -- there is the B/C/S. It's from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, strictly confidential, I won't get into that. It's dated 9 July, as you can see. If that -- maybe bring that up a bit for our eyesight. And it's very urgent to the President of Republika Srpska, for information, the Drina Corps forward command post, Generals Gvero and Krstic personally. And I won't go into the document or read it too much but it's a document that we have become familiar with here. It appears that General Tolimir is passing on information that the president has decided to go forward in the attack on Srebrenica. And can you tell us, General, well, first of all, have you ever seen this before?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, given that it is addressed to the Drina Corps forward command post, Generals Gvero and Krstic personally, what can we tell, if anything, about the location of Generals Gvero and Krstic at the time that this was written?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We submit that this calls for speculation, Your Honour. And in the circumstances, this shouldn't be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You rephrase the question. Does the reference to General Gvero and Krstic indicate their location, and I think -- I think you can rephrase it. I personally -- but I speak for myself, I don't see any problem with the question as is but I'll confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't see any problem. It's a question that doesn't call for any hypothetical answer. It's a straightforward question that can be answered by the general, if he can answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of what I see before me, I don't know the actual state of affairs on the ground, as it was at the time the report was written, but it reads, "To the President of Republika Srpska, for information," you don't know -- you didn't say who-- it was signed, General Tolimir, yes, I can see that. Could you now show the top again? So General Tolimir is responding to some order issued by Karadzic and he's letting Karadzic know that his order is being executed or has been conveyed and is in the process of being carried out. Now, the address is the forward command post of the Drina Corps addressed personally to General Gvero and Krstic. That means that Tolimir knows that they are at the forward command post of the Drina Corps, because if Tolimir had been thinking they were at the Main Staff, it would have been addressed to the Main Staff, not the forward command post out there in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so, given that, and given what you've described about the positions of Generals Gvero and others, can you tell us, if you can, what would -- would Gvero have been there on his own or would he have received orders to go there, in your opinion, or in your view? Based on the military practice at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge -- Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour. We submit this is speculative. The witness wasn't there at the time and he's being asked to assume something which is beyond the scope of his own personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It could become speculative, I agree, but he could also answer the question without speculating, if he can. Go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know whether Gvero was there or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, we have to stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise we will be invading the time of the other Trial Chamber. We'll continue tomorrow. I'm sorry, General, we didn't finish, but there are only a few minutes left, I would presume. And then you're free to go back home. Have you also made up your mind as to what's going to happen? The general can be escorted. Madam Usher, you can escort the general. Thank you. Have you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have discussed the situation with my colleagues, Your Honour. Some of them have no objection to the motion to add documents to the 65 ter list for witness number 4. Others are not sure yet. What the consensus seems to be is that they would prefer witness 4 not testify tomorrow. And I think this has now taken longer than we expected. So the plan is, if it pleases Your Honours, to start off with Witness 165 tomorrow after the general finishes and that will be the only witness for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how long do you anticipate the Simic testimony to last between the two of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If total, I believe it will last less than an hour and a half, an hour to an hour and a half. I will have, unless things go a little bit funny, my direct will be I think about half an hour and my understanding from my friends it's probably the same on cross, maybe a little more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll visit this tomorrow morning. Okay. Thank you. Have a nice afternoon and evening. We'll reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.
